---
title: "Preface"
---

The best way to learn a subject is to teach it. This book, and website, are a
record of my journey to learn music theory through Sonic Pi.

Traditionally, Sonic Pi is presented as a tool to teach programming to students
who are distracted and need enticing by the possibility of making music.
Programming camouflaged as sound generation. This has a number of shortcomings
for an experienced programmer. It forces us to sit through an exposition of what
a loop is, or a thread, or to write code that is repetitive when we can already
easily write a function to parse a musical score written as a list of tuples.

In this book, field notes from my journey into music theory, I want to assume the
programming, and learn the harmony, the melody, the scales, the inversions, and
all the mysterious lore around octaves, and sharps, and flats. If you are like
me, then I hope you will find this text useful.

## How the lessons work

Each lesson takes one musical idea, encodes it as data, plays it, and then asks
you to change something and listen to what happened. Sonic Pi is the laboratory.
The programming stays deliberately ahead of the theory, so what you already know
carries the load.

Six things I decided early, and have not yet regretted:

- **Sound first, name second.** You hear an interval, a cadence, a mode before
  anyone tells you what it is called.
- **Music is data.** A note event carries pitch, onset, duration, amplitude, and
  articulation. Everything else is a function over those.
- **Score and renderer stay separate.** The composition is content. The playback
  function is interpretation. Changing one should not touch the other.
- **Every lesson ends with something worth hearing.** If the last snippet in a
  lesson is a bare test tone, the lesson is broken and I rewrite it.
- **Notation arrives late.** The staff turns up in Part 8, once pitch and
  duration are already familiar as numbers. That makes it a decoding exercise
  rather than a wall.
- **Ear training runs in parallel.** Ten minutes most days, using drills you
  write yourself, from Part 2 onwards.

Ruby idioms get a short note the first time they appear and no more than that.
They are collected in [Ruby for non-Rubyists](appendix/ruby-for-non-rubyists.qmd)
if you are arriving from another language.

Nothing here will teach your hands to play an instrument. What it teaches is what
musicians are doing and why, in a representation you can inspect, test, and
argue with.

## Working rhythm

Four sessions a week gets through the 58 lessons in about fifteen weeks, with the
capstones after that. This is the mix I settled on:

| Session | Length | What |
|---|---|---|
| Two per week | 25 to 35 min | New lessons, in order. |
| One per week | 30 min | Consolidation. Reread the last four lessons and rebuild one example from memory. |
| One per week | 30 min | Free play. Use only what you have met so far and make something you like. |
| Most days | 10 min | Ear drills from your own `drills.rb`. |

Every fourth week, add no new theory. Finish a transcription instead. The theory
sticks when you use it under pressure, and the pressure comes from wanting the
thing to sound right.

## A word on status

Each lesson carries a status. `outline` means the syllabus notes are there and
the prose is not. `draft` means I have written it. `tested` means I have sat down
and worked through it from a cold start, then rewritten it from my own field
notes. Trust the tested ones. Read the drafts knowing they have not survived
contact with a real attempt yet.
